headline: New moon springs flip the switch — sunset flood window back on at Exee Rocks and Stepping Stones
subhead: Bunker schools are stacking off Matinecock again, and the PM flood tide bite that's been missing since the June full moon is finally lining back up with last light.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound settled into that mid-summer rhythm we get every July — warm, a little sloppy on the surface chop from the southwest breeze, and stable underneath. Bay-side water pushed into the high 70s in the back coves — Little Neck Bay and Manhasset Bay both felt more like a bathtub than a fishery by midweek — and that heat did what it always does: it shoved the fluke off the flats and into the channel edges where there's still some cool water moving. Tides were unremarkable, nothing extreme, and the stripers mostly sat on the bottom half of the water column through the day, which is typical for this time of year once the thermocline sets up.

What changes this week is the moon. We're running into a new moon Monday, which means spring tides building right now and bigger water moving through the pinch points — Throgs Neck, Execution Rocks, the Stepping Stones gut. Bigger tides mean more current, and more current means bait gets pushed around and predators get aggressive at the transitions. Here's the piece that matters most: the high stand at Kings Point is lining up with sunset from Friday the 10th through Monday the 13th. That's the first time since the June full moon that we've had a PM flood tide stacking right on top of last light, and that's exactly the window that turns Execution Rocks and Stepping Stones from a daytime pick into a genuine evening program. I'd circle Saturday and Sunday evening on your calendar before anything else this week.

Bunker have been thick off Matinecock Point for going on three weeks now, and they're still there — big pods rolling on the surface an hour before dark, gulls working them from above. That's your tell. Where the bunker sit, the bass and blues aren't far underneath. I've had the best luck working bunker spoons and big paddle-tail swimbaits — the 9-inch Hogy in bunker color — around the edges of the pods rather than dropping right into the middle. Cast past the school, let the lure sink to about 15-18 feet, and swim it back through the deep shadow line under the bait. That's where the better fish are sitting, not up top with the peanut-sized schoolies slashing at the surface.

Live-lining is still the most consistent method if you can net or snag a few bunker off the pod. Fish them on a fish-finder rig, 20-pound fluorocarbon leader, out-of-sight hook, and drift them right along the Execution Rocks rock pile on the outgoing — that current line off the north side has been holding fish all month, and it'll only get better as this spring tide builds through the week. On the incoming, work the same tactic tight to the Stepping Stones light — that's been a proven spring and early-summer striper highway for as long as I've fished this water, and there's no reason for that to change now that the moon's pulling harder.

Bluefish have been the more reliable action honestly, and if you want steady bent rods over trophy numbers, chase the chopper blues instead of hunting bigger bass. They're shredding bunker off Matinecock and up toward Hart Island most mornings, and they'll hit anything that moves fast — Kastmasters, Deadly Dicks, poppers worked hard on the surface. Wire leader is not optional right now; I lost three good topwater plugs last week to blues that bit straight through 40-pound fluoro like it was thread.

Fluke have been a mixed bag, and I'll be straight with you — the bay bite has gone soft as that warm water pushed fish out of the shallow flats in Hempstead Harbor and Manhasset Bay. If you're used to drifting the flats for summer flatfish, shift your thinking to the channel edges and deeper structure instead. The drop-off along the Execution Rocks channel, 25 to 35 feet, has been holding better fish than the flats — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift with the outgoing water. Same story off the deeper humps near Hart Island. Nothing huge — most fish going 16 to 19 inches with the occasional keeper pushing 22 — but a steady pick if you find the right depth and slow your drift down.

Porgies have been solid and honestly a little underrated this time of year. Stepping Stones and the rockpiles off Hart Island are both holding good numbers on sandworms and clam, fished on a simple high-low rig right on bottom. If you want an easy evening with the kids while you wait for the sunset striper window to open, that's your play — steady action, no drama, and it fills a cooler while the tide sets up for the real show.

Weakfish, I'll be honest, are still a no-show. Water's plenty warm enough on paper, but warm water alone has never been the trigger for weakfish in this part of the Sound, and this year is proving that out again. I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now.

Looking ahead — if the wind stays out of the southwest under 10 knots through the weekend, I'd fish the Saturday and Sunday evening flood at Execution Rocks first, Stepping Stones as the backup if the current's running too hard off the rocks. That new moon spring tide combined with the sunset high stand is the best alignment we've had since June, and bunker sitting right on top of both spots makes it worth building your whole weekend around. If the bass don't show on the flood, don't panic — shift to bluefish on the bunker schools at first light off Matinecock. Something's going to eat this week; the question is just which fish shows up first.
